description: We're four students from Dubai competing in person at Sharjah on Dancing with the SARs. We're building an interactive web app using NISAR radar data to show how places in the UAE are changing. Our team brings web development skills in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, a live website launch, and IGCSE studies in Computer Science and ICT. We share an interest in Earth observation and space. We'd welcome remote sensing or GIS knowledge, JavaScript, design or presenting skills.
summary:
OmniSAR is the first game that teaches NASA's new NISAR radar using real NISAR data. We shrank 138 GB of NISAR files into a 32 MB website, over 4,000 times smaller, that runs free in any browser with no login or coding. Every answer is checked against a second source: 86% of our Big Sur burn map sits inside the official fire perimeters.

Players pick one of five real 2026 cases (the Big Sur wildfires, new building in Dubai, flooding at Tonle Sap, sinking ground in Jakarta and farms in Al Ain), sort each piece of evidence as real change or a trap, then compare their call with OmniSAR's measured answer and confidence badge.

It answers Dancing with the SARs directly: every case compares real NISAR passes over time, uses HH and HV polarisations to show what the radar hit, and teaches the traps that fool beginners, such as mountain distortion and interference.

It matters because radar sees through the clouds and smoke that hide floods and fires, yet one NISAR image is about 6 GB, needs a login and coding to open, and is full of traps. OmniSAR lets any student start learning in seconds.
details:
NASA’s new NISAR radar sees through clouds, but almost nobody can use it: each image is almost 6 GB, needs a login and coding to open, and is full of data traps that fake change, which shuts out beginners from a satellite this new. OmniSAR is the first game that teaches NISAR using real NISAR data: we processed 138 GB of NISAR files into a 32 MB website, over 4,000 times smaller, that runs free in any browser with no login, install or coding.

What it does
OmniSAR turns real NISAR radar into five mystery cases from 2026: the Big Sur wildfires (California), new building at Jebel Ali (Dubai), seasonal flooding at Tonle Sap (Cambodia), sinking ground in Jakarta (Indonesia) and farm circles in Al Ain (UAE). You press Play, pick a case, and a real NISAR pass arrives as an alert on a 3D globe. You then sort each piece of evidence as real change, a trap, or “wait for the next pass”. A wrong answer shows the trap that fooled you, using our own data. Finally you make your call and rate your confidence, and OmniSAR reveals its measured answer: for example, 40.4 km² burned at Big Sur and 497.6 hectares of new building at Jebel Ali.

How it works

  1. We searched NASA’s CMR catalogue for NISAR passes before and after each event, then downloaded 55 files (138 GB) from ASF with an Earthdata login.
  2. Python scripts cut out each case area, converted radar power to decibels, reduced speckle and compared passes. Every threshold (for example, “HV fell by at least 2 dB”) was fixed before we saw any result.
  3. Every answer was checked against a second source and given a badge: Strong, Moderate, Weak or Unchecked. 86% of our Big Sur burn map sits inside the official NIFC fire perimeters. Jakarta is rated Weak because the two radar viewing directions agree in only 37 of 99 districts.
  4. The results became small files that the website reads directly, so no number is typed in by hand. Each 3D block’s colour is the average of real NISAR pixels, and heights come from open elevation data.

Benefits

  • No barrier: 32 MB instead of 6 GB per image, with no login and no coding.
  • Learn the traps by falling for them: mountain distortion, interference, speckle, and calm water that looks like dry sand. We found 17 traps in our own data, and each one is shown in the game.
  • Honest answers: every verdict comes with a confidence badge and a full list of the files and steps behind it.

Intended impact
Radar sees through the clouds and smoke that hide floods and fires, and 1.81 billion people face serious flood risk (Rentschler et al., 2022). NISAR images nearly all of Earth’s land every 12 days, for free. OmniSAR helps students, teachers, journalists and local responders learn to read it. Next we plan volcano cases (we’ve already downloaded Kilauea data), a classroom mode in English and Arabic, and a kit that turns any NISAR file into a new case.

Tools and technology

  • Data: NASA NISAR GCOV and GUNW (via ASF and CMR), OPERA, HLS, MODIS, NASA POWER, EONET and GIBS. Partner data: ESA Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2. Also AWS Terrain Tiles and NIFC fire perimeters.
  • Processing: Python, earthaccess and HDF5 tools.
  • Website: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, three.js for the 3D, hosted free on GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: automated browser tests with Playwright.
  • Hardware: a personal laptop.
  • AI: Claude and Claude Code, AI coding assistants, helped write some of the code and debugging and documentation. The idea, design, cases, traps and checks are ours, and there are no AI-generated images or data.

How it’s creative
It allows individuals to access real life situations with real satellite data, to work like an actual scientist and find patterns and solve data problems like a data analyst.

Instead of a dashboard for experts, it’s a game where you make the call yourself. The Earth is drawn in blocks, where each block averages many real radar pixels; this keeps the site light and smooths the radar’s grainy speckle. Burned forest flashes red and new buildings flash cyan as the passes replay on their real dates.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: rules fixed before results, a second source for every case, and Weak or Unchecked badges where the data can’t decide.
  • No future data: the game never shows a pass dated after the event you’re solving.
  • Accessibility: runs on any laptop, playable by keyboard, and flashing kept at 3 times a second or slower (a seizure-safety limit).
  • Privacy: no accounts, and no personal data collected.
